article.overview: A subsurface imaging system is an instrument class that maps layers, buried reflecting boundaries and other structures beneath the lunar surface without excavating them. The lunar examples discussed here are radar systems: a transmitter sends radio signals into the ground, and a receiver records the echoes returned from the surface and from buried interfaces. The catalogue entry describes a measurement function rather than one standard design, so this article covers several flown and proposed instruments that address that function. Their specifications differ substantially, and none should be read as representative of the whole class. [2][8]
article.description: The term covers instruments that produce images or structural maps of the subsurface. In this article it is used for radar sounders and ground-penetrating radars that operate either from lunar orbit or from a surface vehicle. Radar sounding relies on the fact that radio waves are partly reflected where electrical properties change, for example between regolith layers, between lava flows, or at the base of a buried deposit [1][5]. Depending on frequency, transmitted power and antenna design, the signal may penetrate hundreds of metres or several kilometres, but longer-wavelength systems resolve less detail. Surface-based ground-penetrating radar gives finer resolution over shallower depths [7]. Related catalogue entries, including ground-penetrating radar, lunar penetrating radar, subsurface radar sounder, borehole imaging system and lunar subsurface tomography system, address overlapping measurement goals. They are not described in this article.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Subsurface imaging instruments are used to determine the layering, thickness and structure of the lunar crust and regolith. The Apollo 17 sounder's stated objectives included mapping subsurface electrical structure, and its design goal was to probe the upper 2 km of the crust [2][3]. The Kaguya Lunar Radar Sounder was designed for subsurface radar sounding together with natural plasma-wave observation [4][5]. The Deep Wave Radar proposal states that it is expected to help search for resources such as water ice and to support site selection for habitats. That is a design aim, not a demonstrated result [7]. Applications include mapping buried lava flows and impact deposits, estimating regolith depth for engineering and resource studies, and identifying subsurface interfaces that could guide later drilling or sampling. The last application is a suggestion rather than a documented outcome of a specific instrument.
article.operating_principle: A radar sounder transmits a signal into the ground and measures the delay and strength of the returning echoes. Because radio waves travel through the ground at a finite speed, the delay gives an estimate of depth once a propagation speed for the material has been assumed. Longer wavelengths generally penetrate further but resolve less detail. This trade-off drove the choice of several frequencies for the Apollo instrument, which used wavelengths of about 60, 20 and 2 m, as summarised in the abstract of Porcello et al. (1974) [2][3]. Orbital systems add a synthetic-aperture step: as the spacecraft moves along its track, many echoes are combined to form a finer along-track image. The Apollo system recorded its returns on 70 mm film for processing after the mission [3]. Surface clutter, meaning echoes from the rough surface itself, can mask weaker subsurface reflections, and earlier analyses of Apollo data reduced this effect by comparing successive orbits [3]. The Lunar Radar Sounder operated at a 5 MHz radar frequency and also observed natural radio and plasma waves [4]. Dielectric properties also matter: dry, low-loss material lets long wavelengths penetrate much further than wet or conductive material would [3].
article.scientific_importance: Orbital sounding is valuable because it samples large areas and buried structures that surface instruments cannot reach. The NASA preliminary science report on the Apollo experiment states that preliminary subsurface analysis suggested the instrument could achieve its substrate-sounding goal [1]. Later interpretations of Apollo data proposed subsurface reflectors beneath Mare Serenitatis and Mare Crisium and estimated basalt thickness in Mare Crisium [3]. These are model-dependent interpretations from a secondary source and should be treated with caution. The Kaguya LRS abstract reports distinct reflectors at depths of several hundred metres in the nearside maria [5]. Subsurface imaging matters for resource assessment, for engineering of landing and construction sites, and for understanding how the lunar crust was built up by volcanic and impact processes.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a subsurface imaging system. The examples below comprise a historical orbital radar sounder, a second orbital sounder, a compact P-band synthetic-aperture radar that is still in development, and a proposed rover-mounted ground-penetrating radar. They use different frequencies, antennas, platforms and mission roles, so their values are not directly comparable and should not be tabulated against one another.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions are instrument-specific and were not published in a complete form for any example in the sources reviewed. The LRS relies on two sets of 30 m tip-to-tip dipole antennas [4], so antenna geometry dominates its physical envelope. The Apollo sounder's antennas and electronics were part of the Apollo spacecraft configuration, with the electronics housed in the Apollo Service Module [3]. Dimensions for SESAR-LITE and the Deep Wave Radar were not stated in the reviewed sources. Antenna length is therefore one of the most important differences between the examples.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass is published for only some examples. The ALSE total system mass of 43 kg comes from a secondary source [3]. The JAXA specification table for the LRS lists 23.182 kg [4]. These two figures should not be compared without checking what each includes. No mass was found for SESAR-LITE or the Deep Wave Radar in the sources reviewed.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power is also instrument-specific. The ALSE secondary source reports a total power draw of 103 W [3]. The LRS specification table lists 56.7 W of power and 800 W of radiated power during radar transmission [4]. Radiated RF power is not the same as the electrical power drawn from the host spacecraft, and the two must not be conflated. Power figures for SESAR-LITE and the Deep Wave Radar are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Subsurface radars must survive the lunar vacuum, large thermal cycles, radiation and fine dust. Orbital radars need antennas that can be accommodated or deployed on the spacecraft; the LRS used two 30 m tip-to-tip dipole sets [4]. Surface ground-penetrating radars need controlled coupling to the ground, management of interference from the host vehicle, and accurate timing. Radar depth estimates depend on the dielectric properties of regolith and rock, which change with temperature, moisture and composition, so depth estimates need uncertainty allowances. Operational requirements also include recording or telemetry capacity: the LRS specification lists 492 kbps high-speed and 176 kbps low-speed telemetry [4], while the Apollo sounder relied on film recording [3].
article.limitations: The main limitations are the penetration-resolution trade-off, surface clutter, sensitivity to dielectric assumptions and the dependence on large antennas and heavy processing. Orbital sounders observe large areas at the cost of spatial detail and cannot directly verify their interpretations. Surface systems resolve more detail, but only along their traverse and usually to shallower depths. The ALSE depth estimates and channel values come from a secondary source and should not be treated as an authoritative specification. A reflector depth from a radar sounder is a model result that depends on assumed propagation speed. Interpretation also needs ground truth from cores, boreholes or complementary geophysics, which the sources reviewed did not supply for these examples [3][5].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The transportation method depends on the platform. The Apollo and Kaguya sounders were orbital instruments and did not land as such, so their relevant interfaces are spacecraft integration, lunar orbit insertion and data downlink. The Deep Wave Radar is a surface-mobility instrument proposed for a rover-mounted role. SESAR-LITE is aimed at small launch opportunities, but no host spacecraft is named in the source reviewed [6][7].
transportation_process: Integrate the radar with its host spacecraft or rover on Earth, including antenna stowage, thermal interfaces and electrical interfaces.
Launch the host vehicle and transfer to the Moon. For orbiting systems, insert into lunar orbit and commission the antennas and recorders.
For surface systems, deliver the instrument with a lander or rover, release it from the host, and deploy and check the antenna.
Operate with pointing, power, thermal and data interfaces to the host, and downlink or record the echo data for analysis.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Orbital sounders do not deploy onto the surface, but their antennas must be deployed or configured in orbit. The LRS source does not describe its antenna deployment mechanism in the page reviewed. For the Apollo sounder, the Apollo 17 Command and Service Module carried the instrument, and the film was retrieved by an astronaut during an extravehicular activity on the return flight [3]. A surface Deep Wave Radar would need a deployment and coupling method that is not described in the reviewed source [7].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 17 Apollo Lunar Sounder Experiment flew in lunar orbit on the Command and Service Module [2][3]. The Kaguya (SELENE) Lunar Radar Sounder operated from a JAXA lunar orbiter and combined radar sounding with natural plasma-wave observation [4][5]. No surface subsurface-imaging flight with a verified lander interface was identified in the sources reviewed.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No verified lander, rover or spacecraft interface was found for SESAR-LITE or the Deep Wave Radar. The DLR page links the Deep Wave Radar to the L-MAPS instrument on a future Lunar Terrain Vehicle in the Artemis context [7], but no interface document was reviewed. Compatibility is therefore not asserted. Any future assessment would need the radar's mass, dimensions, mounting, loads, power, data and deployment requirements compared against verified vehicle specifications.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 17 Apollo Lunar Sounder Experiment is an early example of a radar sounder operated from lunar orbit. Its significance lies in showing that radar could return information about structure beneath the lunar surface [1][3]. The Kaguya Lunar Radar Sounder extended this approach with a modern orbital sounder that combined subsurface sounding with passive plasma-wave observation [4][5]. The SESAR-LITE and Deep Wave Radar concepts show a shift toward compact, surface-compatible imaging, but both remain under development or proposed [6][7]. The historical record should be read with caution, because the instruments measured different quantities and the Apollo interpretations depend on processing methods that are decades old [3].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Several key values are unresolved. The ALSE mass, power, channel parameters and depth estimates come from a single secondary source, and the 1974 Proceedings of the IEEE paper was not read in full. The ALSE frequencies differ between the text and the table in that source. The LRS sounding depth is 5 km in the JAXA table and several kilometres in its text. The Ono et al. (2010) full text was not accessed, so its statements are taken from the abstract only. The LRS along-track resolution is not stated on the source page reviewed. SESAR-LITE and the Deep Wave Radar do not publish mass, power or antenna figures in the sources reviewed. No example has verified lander compatibility. Image provenance and verification status are recorded in the JSON image notes.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. The DLR source page is the clean canonical permalink (the original ?p= form was not used). Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: ALSE total mass (43 kg), power (103 W), channel table, penetration estimates, antenna description and film-recording details come from the Wikipedia ALSE article, a secondary source. The primary Porcello et al. (1974) Proceedings of the IEEE paper was only seen as an abstract, so these values are unverified against primary literature.

ALSE frequencies conflict within the secondary source: text gives 5, 15 and 150 MHz; table gives 5.266, 15.8 and 158 MHz. Unresolved. The approximate wavelengths of 60, 20 and 2 m are from the IEEE abstract as summarised in search results.
The LRS sounding depth is 5 km in the JAXA specification table and 'within a depth of several km' in the JAXA body text. Both are reported; neither is resolved.
The LRS along-track resolution is not stated on the JAXA page reviewed. Along-track values surfaced in search excerpts were not confirmed on the source page and are excluded.

The Ono et al. (2010) Space Science Reviews paper was not accessed in full (Springer full text redirected to an authentication page). Its nearside-maria reflector statement is taken from the abstract only.

The JAXA image img_lrs_003_e.gif is associated on the JAXA page with an antenna caption, but its visible content is an observation-geometry illustration. The article caption follows the image content.
The JAXA image img_lrs_004_e.gif is a synthesised example per its alt text, not a measured dataset. It is labelled as such in the article.

The ALSE radar image (Wikimedia Commons, NASA) is a secondary-mirror image. Commons licence metadata records public domain (NASA); it is not traced to an original NASA archive record. It is the only image not from an official agency page.

SESAR-LITE mass, power, dimensions, antenna size, resolution value, TRL and flight status are not publicly specified in the NTRS record reviewed. No images were verified for SESAR-LITE, so none are included.
The Deep Wave Radar page gives no numeric mass, power, dimensions, frequency range or depth. Its images are engineering models. Source text is German and was translated for the captions.
No example has verified lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility. The transportation section therefore makes no compatibility claim, and the transportation image array is empty.
The lunar location recommendations are deferred by the user and are not included.
Full-resolution image downloads were not checked. Image URLs were checked for HTTP 200 responses and inspected at the resolution served.

Related catalogue entries (ground-penetrating radar, lunar penetrating radar, subsurface radar sounder, borehole imaging system, lunar subsurface tomography system) are named but not described, and no facts from other payloads were reused.
